notes.meaning: God himself says he will stir up a destroyer against Babylon. "Leb-kamai" is a code name for Chaldea, Babylon's land. It means "the heart of those who rise against me." Babylon was the center of God's enemies, because it had cruelly treated his people. The destroyer is the army of the Medes and Persians. God needs only a breath of wind to sweep his enemies away.

To "winnow" means to toss grain into the wind so the light, useless chaff blows away. Babylon will be blown away like chaff and her land emptied. Babylon had once winnowed God's people. Now the same thing happens to her. Enemies on every side mean there is no way to escape.

Older translations read the first words in two ways. Some take them as a call to the attacking archers to fight hard. Others take them as a warning to Babylon's archers that fighting back is useless. Either way, the point is clear. The invaders are told not to spare Babylon's young soldiers, and her whole army will be wiped out.
Babylon's people will fall dead all through the land. They will die not only in the open fields but in the city streets too. Babylon's great armies will not save her.

Israel and Judah are pictured as a wife whose husband is not dead. God has not left them like widows forever. Their land was full of sin, and God rightly let enemies punish them. Still, he treats them better than they deserve and keeps his covenant, his binding promise to them. Some older writers read "their land" as Babylon's land, full of guilt for fighting against God.

God's people living in Babylon are warned to run for their lives. They should not be caught up in the punishment for Babylon's sins. God has set times for judging the wicked. He may seem slow, but the time has come, and he will pay Babylon back.

Babylon was rich and splendid, like a gold cup. God held that cup in his hand and used Babylon to pour out his anger on other nations. Those nations suffered so much that they acted like people drunk or out of their minds. The book of Revelation uses the same picture for a later "Babylon."
Babylon's fall comes all at once. God can do in a moment what he has decided. The call to bring balm, a healing ointment, is said with irony. No medicine can cure Babylon's wound.

Many old writers hear Babylon's allies and hired soldiers speaking here. They tried to save her, saw it was hopeless, and went home. Others hear God's captive people, who had tried to turn Babylon from its idols and failed. Her judgment "reaching the sky" means it is so great that no help under heaven can stop it.

Now God's people speak. "Vindication" means God has shown their cause was right. It does not mean they earned it. Babylon had been a cruel bully toward them, and God took their side. So they want to go to Zion, God's holy city Jerusalem, and tell others what he has done.

God stirs the hearts of the kings of the Medes, Darius and Cyrus, to come against Babylon. God rules even the minds of kings to carry out his plan. Babylon is being paid back for the wrong done to his people and his temple. The call to sharpen arrows may be a taunt to Babylon, as if to say "Get ready, but it won't help." It may also be a call to the attackers.

Many old writers take this as a mocking call to Babylon. They read it as saying: put up your flags, post your guards, set your traps. All of it will fail. God had planned Babylon's fall and he will surely do what he said. Some read it as orders to the attacking army instead.

The great Euphrates River split into many channels around Babylon. That made the city hard to attack and helped make it rich. Yet neither her rivers nor her wealth can save her. The picture of a thread being cut comes from weaving. When cloth is finished, it is cut off the loom. God is putting an end to Babylon's greed.

God makes a promise under oath, swearing by himself because there is no one greater. This removes all doubt. Babylon had huge numbers of people, but the invaders will be even more, like a swarm of locusts. They will win easily and shout for joy, as people did at harvest time.

Verses 15 to 19 repeat words from Jeremiah 10:12-16. Here they remind God's people who is promising Babylon's fall. He made the earth, set the world in order and spread out the sky. So nothing is too hard for him, not even breaking mighty Babylon.

God rules the thunder, rain, clouds, lightning and wind. Babylon boasted of sitting by many waters. But God can make "many waters" just by speaking. Wind and weather may have natural causes, but God is behind them all.

People who make idols are foolish to think their skill can make a god. A lump of gold or a piece of wood does not become divine by being shaped. These idols have no breath, no life at all. Only God is the source of life.

Idols are empty and worth nothing. They only trick people. When God comes to judge, they will be shown to be nothing and will perish. This was meant to help God's people wait patiently while idol-worshiping Babylon still looked strong.

"The Portion of Jacob" is God himself, the treasure that belongs to his people. He is nothing like the idols, because he made everything. His people are also his own special possession. They belong to each other. He is the LORD of Hosts, the God of all power.

Many old writers see Babylon as the war club here. God had used Babylon as his hammer to smash nations, armies, horses and chariots. Even so, Babylon will be judged in turn. Being God's tool against others does not keep anyone safe from his judgment. Some older writers think the club means the Medes and Persians or Cyrus. Others think it means Nebuchadnezzar, Babylon's king.
